title: Longer Disciplined Tapers Improve Marathon Performance for Recreational Runners
journal: Frontiers in Sports and Active Living
population: More than 158,000 recreational marathon runners with logged training activities
findings: More than 158,000 recreational marathon runners analysed; tapers defined from decreases in weekly distance and classified by duration (1-4 weeks) and discipline (strict = progressively decreasing training in the weeks before the marathon; relaxed = not).
Strict tapers were associated with better marathon performance than relaxed tapers (p < 0.001); longer tapers of up to 3 weeks were associated with better performance than shorter tapers (p < 0.001).
Strict 3-week tapers were associated with a median finish-time saving of 5 min 32.4 s (2.6%) compared with a minimal taper (p < 0.001).
Female runners were associated with greater finish-time benefits than men for a given taper type (<= 3 weeks in duration), p < 0.001.
Most recreational runners (64%) adopt less disciplined (2-week and 3-week) tapers.
limitations: Observational and self-selected, so strict tapers may travel with other differences (fitness, discipline, injury-free build-up); taper identified from weekly distance only; associations in median finish times, not causal effects; the abstract does not report what happened for 4-week tapers beyond 'up to 3 weeks'.
implications: For marathon plans, default to a 3-week strict taper: each of the three final weeks lower in volume than the previous one (monotonic decrease), not a flat reduction.
Add a plan validation rule that flags a taper whose weekly volumes are not monotonically decreasing.

Cap the marathon taper at 3 weeks. The abstract supports benefit 'up to 3 weeks' but does not say 4 weeks is worse, so the cap is a conservative engine choice also supported by bosquet-2007 and aubry-2014 (peaks within first 2 taper weeks).
Female/male difference is an association only; no separate sex parameter is justified, but sex-specific messaging could note it.

verification.notes: Crossref matches (Frontiers, 28 Sep 2021, Smyth first author). Researcher's claim 'data show no further benefit and risk of detraining' beyond 3 weeks is NOT in the abstract and was removed; data-source description ('public/wearable-style') also not in the abstract so generalised.
